In a Turkish high school, a thousand students practised their maths. A third of them had ChatGPT.
With it, practice scores rose forty-eight percent. Then the exam, without it: seventeen percent lower than students who never had it.
The worry is old. Twenty-four centuries ago, a king refused writing itself: it would create forgetfulness in the learners' souls.
Calculators were accused too: seventy-nine studies later, children who used them did better by hand. Autopilot was accused, and the regulators agreed.
In the famous brain study, none of eighteen ChatGPT writers could quote their own essay. But fifty-four people is small, and the authors said: do not call it dumber.
Reading an answer four times beats being tested, for five minutes. A week later the tested learner keeps sixty-one percent; the reader, forty.
Effort builds memory; fluency only feels like it. Developers with AI tools were nineteen percent slower, and believed they were twenty percent faster.
And everyone drifts together. Stories written with AI ideas got a little better, and a lot more alike.
The same model, told to give hints and never answers, lifted practice a hundred and twenty-seven percent, and the exam penalty disappeared.
Not dumber. Worse at whatever you let it do for you, and unable to feel it. Use it so that if it vanished tomorrow, you could still think.
